items.title: Albert Nicholas Interview, 1972-06-26
items.q: We had Red Island, Otis Johnson, and Hemp Hill, and Louis. It was four trumpets...

ctx.x: Did you, well which sax did you play with, say Louis Russell?

I played third alto. I played first alto. Charlie Holmes was on third. And Tenny Hill when I joined the band in 29, was on tenor. Then later on we had two tenors and two altos. I played for about two years alto. Then it changed me to tenor. And I played first tenor when Greely Walton came in the band. I was playing alto when Greely came. Then we marched in the band with four, with four. And Louis came in the band. Then I went on first tenor. I played until 1940. I'd switch up and down. Sometime I'd play alto,…
That's not the same George Washington that was down here in New Orleans.

items.title: Albert Nicholas Interview, 1967-02-09
items.q: I was in the band when they sent for Red from New Orleans. I was in the band when we sent for him, yes, when he came to join Louis Russell's band.

ctx.x: Well, to move to another great musician, a great band of musicians, when you were with Louis Russell, you must have had a tremendous, you were nine? Nine of us there. How many years were you there? Ten years. A little over ten years. Getting back to another musician from New Orleans or just outside, Henry Red Allen, you must have played a lot with him in those years, with the Louis Russell band. He was with them what, four years?

I was in the band when they sent for Red from New Orleans. I was in the band when we sent for him, yes, when he came to join Louis Russell's band. And you had so many good bands in New York at the time, organized bands, and we were just one of another band. But we had an original style of our own, because Duke even told Louis Russell, you must always keep that style.
But I mean, when Louis Armstrong and Red Allen were in the band together, did they each take solos together?

items.title: Albert Nicholas Interview, 1972-06-26
items.q: we sent him and got Lee when Red Allen came in the band... See, we had two bands... then we go with Red Allen... That's where Red would get off

ctx.x: Were your arrangements easy to play?

Well, you'd get used to them, yeah. You'd get used to them, sure. We'd take, when we came off the road from the least one night, as we'd go on the road saying, Joe Green would build a tune for us for two months. The Easton tune, the Western tune, and the Southern tune, and all that sort of stuff. When we'd come back, we'd buy new arrangements, different tunes. Now, we'd take a number. The reeds would get into this side of the hall, or wherever we were rehearsing. The brass gets over, the trombones get over there,…
You think he was the man that we'd do? What Lewis could read, man. Don't let nobody kid you.
